THOUGHT: The presentation fits a degenerative (mechanical) process more than a primary inflammatory arthritis. Key supportive points: age 67, pain that improves with rest (mechanical pattern), unilateral knee swelling with reduced ROM from pain, and knee x‑ray showing joint space narrowing and subchondral sclerosis without erosions — classic osteoarthritis (OA) changes. Negative RF and anti-CCP make rheumatoid arthritis unlikely, and the absence of systemic features or fever makes septic arthritis less likely (but aspiration would be indicated if concern persists). Elevated ESR/CRP indicate some ongoing inflammation but can be seen with acute synovitis on top of OA or with other comorbidity; they do not by themselves confirm RA. Nail pitting and “dandruff” raise the possibility of psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis, which can be seronegative and asymmetric, but there is no reported psoriatic skin disease, no erosive/pencil‑in‑cup x‑ray changes, and no sacroiliitis to support that diagnosis. Crystal arthropathy (e.g., pseudogout) could present acutely in an elderly knee but no chondrocalcinosis is reported and the radiographic pattern aligns with chronic degenerative change. Overall the most likely single diagnosis accounting for the history, exam, and x‑ray is degenerative osteoarthritis of the right knee; consider joint aspiration if clinical concern for infection or crystal disease persists, and assess for possible coexisting inflammatory or psoriatic disease given nail findings.

DIAGNOSIS: Osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease) of the right knee.
